query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the feedstock particle size distribution for FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy thermal-spray deposition from 15–45 μm to 30–75 μm will yield a bond coat with at least a 30% improvement in coating thickness while maintaining coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation compared to the standard feedstock.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder feedstock with particle sizes in the 15–45 μm range, exhibiting characteristics typical of thermal-spray processed powders.
generation.intervention: Replace the existing powder feedstock with one that has a controlled particle size distribution shifted to 30–75 μm, keeping all other spray process parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Deposition using atmospheric plasma spraying under standard conditions (fixed spray distance, gas flows, and substrate preparation) and service conditions typical for bond coats in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.structural_mediator: The larger powder particles will generate thicker splats upon impact due to higher melting thermal mass and momentum, which leads to increased layer build-up and a denser coating structure with fewer oxide inclusions.
generation.mechanism: Larger particles reduce the relative surface area exposed to the high-temperature, oxygen-rich environment during flight, thereby limiting oxidation. Their greater mass and momentum promote enhanced splat formation and inter-splat bonding, resulting in a thicker, more contiguous deposit while preserving the desired microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention will produce a FeCoNiCrAl bond coat with a coating thickness increased by at least 30% relative to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock) while maintaining comparable levels of as-sprayed oxidation and microstructural integrity.
generation.baseline: Bond coats produced using the 15–45 μm feedstock, which exhibit insufficient thickness and standard levels of in-flight oxidation leading to suboptimal deposition efficiency.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected to hold as long as the particle size distribution remains within the 30–75 μm range and other spray parameters (e.g., plasma temperature, spray distance, and gas environment) are unaltered. If the particles become too large, incomplete melting or poor adhesion may occur.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the optimum upper limit of the particle size distribution for complete melting, potential adjustments needed in spray parameters to accommodate the new feedstock, and the precise quantitative improvement in thickness, which may vary with minor process variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a comparative experiment depositing FeCoNiCrAl bond coats using two feedstock distributions: the baseline (15–45 μm) and the modified (30–75 μm) under identical atmospheric plasma spray conditions. Evaluate coating thickness, oxidation state via XRD/EDS, microstructural integrity via SEM, and adhesion via pull-off testing.
measurements: Oxidation levels (assessed using XRD and EDS for oxide phase quantification)
Adhesion strength (measured via standard pull-off tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating deposited with the larger (30–75 μm) feedstock does not show at least a 30% increase in thickness compared to the 15–45 μm baseline, or if it exhibits significantly higher levels of oxidation or reduced adhesion, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) deposited by thermal spray (HVOF)
papers.approach: Using gas‐atomized powder in thermal spray; analysis of in‐flight oxidation and phase transformations as a function of spraying distance and processing temperature.
papers.findings: Smaller particles tend to experience extensive in‐flight oxidation, whereas larger particles show surface oxidation only. Increased spraying distance raises the α-Al2O3 content but does not necessarily improve microhardness.
papers.mechanism: High heating rates in the spray process cause rapid melting and oxidation; particle surface area plays a critical role with smaller particles oxidizing more completely due to a higher surface area to volume ratio.

papers.title: Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA used as a feedstock for atmospheric plasma spraying (APS)
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying to produce feedstock powders (with particle sizes initially in the ~15–45 μm range) deposited via APS and subsequent microstructural and phase analysis of the coating.
papers.findings: The original lamellar structure of the milled powder transforms during spraying—resulting in nanocrystalline grains. However, the as-deposited coating thickness is limited, which is partly related to the feedstock characteristics.
papers.mechanism: Feedstock particle size and morphology affect melting, splat formation, and deposition efficiency; smaller feedstock particles can melt too rapidly and form thinner deposits, while excessive oxidation is promoted by high specific surface area.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlFe HEA coatings deposited on 316L stainless steel via APS
papers.approach: APS deposition followed by annealing, with microstructural, phase, and corrosion characterizations.
papers.findings: As-sprayed coatings exhibit a mixture of BCC/FCC phases with evidence of in-flight oxidation (including formation of spinel oxides), which affects properties like corrosion resistance and hardness.
papers.mechanism: High-temperature plasma jet conditions cause rapid melting and oxidation; control of oxidation is critical for coating integrity in service environments.

papers.title: Microparticles of High Entropy Alloys Made by Laser-Induced Forward Transfer.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA coatings prepared via a LIFT process
papers.approach: Utilization of ultra-short laser pulses to transfer HEA films in the microparticle range; analysis of particle morphology and oxidation state.
papers.findings: Microparticles with sizes above a critical value (<5 μm particles are fully oxidized) can preserve a primarily metallic core with only surface oxidation, suggesting that particle size is key to limiting oxidation while maintaining coating integrity.
papers.mechanism: Larger particle sizes reduce the relative surface area subject to in-flight oxidation, preserving the core composition while allowing controlled deposition.

established: Thermal spray processes subject HEA feedstock particles to rapid heating and cooling, which leads to significant in-flight oxidation.
Smaller feedstock particles (with higher surface area-to-volume ratios) are more prone to full oxidation, while larger particles tend to retain a metallic core with superficial oxidation.
Coating thickness and deposition efficiency depend critically on feedstock characteristics (particle size, morphology) and process parameters.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing processing parameters (spray distance, plasma jet temperature, and powder feed rate) in APS and HVOF
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved deposition quality and microstructure control, but limited success in achieving sufficient coating thickness when using 15–45 μm feedstock, with persistent issues of in-flight oxidation.

approaches_tried.approach: Pre-alloying and mechanical alloying to adjust particle microstructure prior to spraying
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced coating adhesion and formation of desired solid solution phases; however, the coating thickness remained below the target when using small feedstock sizes.

mechanisms: Feedstock particle size influences melting behavior and oxidation; larger particles have lower specific surface area leading to reduced oxidation.
In-flight oxidation is driven by high temperatures and oxygen-rich environments during thermal spray, affecting both phase formation and coating integrity.
Deposition efficiency (and thus coating thickness) is closely tied to the dynamics of particle melting, splat formation, and kinetic energy upon impact.
disagreements: While some studies indicate that higher energy inputs or smaller particle sizes can improve melting and splat formation, these parameters often simultaneously increase oxidation, leading to a trade-off between deposition efficiency and coating oxidation.

Different thermal spray methods (APS vs. HVOF) yield distinct oxidation levels even with similar feedstock sizes, suggesting that the ideal feedstock size and processing window may vary between techniques.
open_questions: Can a single intervention on feedstock selection (e.g., increasing average particle size beyond 45 μm) achieve both the required coating thickness and minimal as-sprayed oxidation?
What is the optimal balance between increased feedstock size, deposition efficiency, and oxidation control in the thermal spray process for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats?
How do alterations in feedstock size interact with process parameters (spray distance, gas flow, temperature) to affect overall coating integrity in service conditions?
opportunities: Investigate using a controlled increase in the feedstock particle size distribution (e.g., shifting from 15–45 μm to 30–75 μm) to enhance deposition rate and achieve thicker coatings without increasing oxidation.
Combine feedstock size optimization with fine-tuning of spray parameters (such as shorter in-flight residence time and lower oxygen partial pressure) to preserve coating integrity.
Develop experiments that systematically vary only the feedstock particle size in otherwise identical thermal spray conditions to directly test its impact on coating thickness and oxidation.

directions.direction: Increase the feedstock powder particle size distribution from 15–45 μm to approximately 30–75 μm.
directions.assessment: This intervention directly addresses the thickness shortfall by increasing the particle mass and momentum during impact, which enhances splat formation and deposition efficiency while reducing the relative surface area available for oxidation. The established literature (e.g., PMC9694738 and PMC5849017) supports the notion that larger particles reduce in-flight oxidation, thereby preserving coating integrity. This strategy is highly feasible, minimally disruptive to other process parameters, and directly leverages known physics of thermal spray deposition.

directions.direction: Optimize spray process parameters such as powder feed rate and stand-off distance.
directions.assessment: Altering process parameters could potentially increase deposition rate; however, these modifications can exacerbate in-flight oxidation or create uneven splat formation. While they respect the oxidation and integrity constraints, the benefit on coating thickness may not be as robust as modifying the feedstock.

directions.direction: Introduce an inert gas shroud or reduce oxygen partial pressure around the spray plume.
directions.assessment: This method would help minimize oxidation, preserving coating integrity. However, it does not directly enhance thickness deposition and might require additional equipment or process complexity.

directions.direction: Preheat the feedstock powder prior to injection into the spray plume.
directions.assessment: Preheating could modify particle melting dynamics to favor thicker splat formation. However, controlling preheating uniformly without inducing unwanted oxidation adds complexity, and the direct impact on thickness improvement is less clear.

directions.direction: Incorporate minor alloying additions that act as oxidation inhibitors in the HEA feedstock.
directions.assessment: While adding elements that lower oxidation kinetics can help preserve coating integrity, this approach may alter the alloy’s phase stability and does not directly solve a low deposition efficiency issue that causes the shortfall in thickness.

choice.direction: Increase the feedstock powder particle size distribution from 15–45 μm to approximately 30–75 μm.
choice.why: This single intervention directly targets the known correlation between particle size and deposition efficiency. Larger particles have a lower surface area-to-volume ratio, which reduces in-flight oxidation while providing greater momentum upon substrate impact. This enhances splat formation and results in a thicker, more robust coating—all under the same spray conditions. The approach is supported by established studies (e.g., PMC9694738 and PMC5849017) and is both feasible and minimally disruptive to the overall process.
